text: Every weather forecast starts from a picture of the atmosphere right now.
say: Every weather forecast starts from a picture of the atmosphere right now.
heard: Every weather forecast starts from a picture of the atmosphere right now.

text: But nobody can see right now. Stations dot the land. Balloons rise twice a day. Satellites sweep past in narrow stripes.
say: But nobody can see right now. Stations dot the land. Balloons rise twice a day. Satellites sweep past in narrow stripes.
heard: But nobody can see right now. Stations dot the land. Balloons rise twice a day. Satellites sweep past in narrow stripes.

text: Turning those scattered clues into one picture is the slow, expensive step that every forecast waits for.
say: Turning those scattered clues into one picture is the slow, expensive step that every forecast waits for.
heard: Turning those scattered clues into one picture is the slow, expensive step that every forecast waits for.

text: So here is the question. Can a machine learn to see the present, with no answer key?
say: So here is the question. Can a machine learn to see the present, with no answer key?
heard: So here is the question. Can a machine learn to see the present with no answer key?

text: This paper, by Kate Duffy and her colleagues at Zeus AI, builds a world model that learns from the observations alone.
say: This paper, by Kate Duffy and her colleagues at Zeus AI, builds a world model that learns from the observations alone.
heard: This paper by Kate Duffy and her colleagues at Zeus AI, builds a world model that learns from the observations alone.

text: Start with the clues. About eleven thousand surface stations report every hour, but only on land, and only near the ground.
say: Start with the clues. About eleven thousand surface stations report every hour, but only on land, and only near the ground.
heard: Start with the clues. About 11,000 surface stations report every hour, but only on land and only near the ground.

text: About six hundred and fifty weather balloons climb through the whole atmosphere, twice a day.
say: About six hundred and fifty weather balloons climb through the whole atmosphere, twice a day.
heard: About 650, weather balloons climb through the whole atmosphere twice a day.

text: And satellites see nearly everything, but they don't measure temperature or wind. They measure light, glowing from a deep column of air.
say: And satellites see nearly everything, but they don't measure temperature or wind. They measure light, glowing from a deep column of air.
heard: And satellites see nearly everything, but they don't measure temperature or wind. They measure light, glowing from a deep column of air.

text: Sparse, irregular, indirect.
say: Sparse, irregular, indirect.
heard: Sparse, irregular, indirect.

text: Turning clues into a full state of the atmosphere is called data assimilation. Its output is the analysis.
say: Turning clues into a full state of the atmosphere is called data assimilation. Its output is the analysis.
heard: Turning clues into a full state of the atmosphere is called data assimilation. Its output is the analysis.

text: Global centres run it every six hours, with hand-built models for every instrument, and the result arrives hours late.
say: Global centres run it every six hours, with hand-built models for every instrument, and the result arrives hours late.
heard: Global centers run it every six hours, with hand-built models for every instrument, and the result arrives hours late.

text: Machine learning forecasters now rival the physics models. But most of them start from that physics-built analysis.
say: Machine learning forecasters now rival the physics models. But most of them start from that physics-built analysis.
heard: Machine learning forecasters now rival the physics models, but most of them start from that physics-built analysis.

text: They learned to forecast. They never learned to see.
say: They learned to forecast. They never learned to see.
heard: They learned to forecast. They never learned to see.

text: Assimilation is a loop: predict, then correct.
say: Assimilation is a loop: predict, then correct.
heard: Assimilation is a loop. Predict, then correct.

text: Run the last analysis forward to get a background, the forecast of now.
say: Run the last analysis forward to get a background, the forecast of now.
heard: Run the last analysis forward to get a background, the forecast of now.

text: Compare it with new observations, and move toward them by a gain.
say: Compare it with new observations, and move toward them by a gain.
heard: Compare it with new observations and move toward them by a gain.

text: Say the forecast reads twenty degrees and a thermometer twenty-two. If the thermometer is the more reliable of the two, move most of the way.
say: Say the forecast reads twenty degrees and a thermometer twenty-two. If the thermometer is the more reliable of the two, move most of the way.
heard: Say the forecast reads 20 degrees and a thermometer 22. If the thermometer is the more reliable of the two, move most of the way.

text: Rudolf Kalman wrote this down in 1960. Operational systems still set every error by hand.
say: Rudolf Kahlman wrote this down in 1960. Operational systems still set every error by hand.
heard: Rudolph Kalman wrote this down in 1960. Operational systems still set every error by hand.

text: This model learns every piece of that loop instead.
say: This model learns every piece of that loop instead.
heard: This model learns every piece of that loop instead.

text: Each cell of a fifty kilometre grid carries a wide memory, five hundred and twelve numbers, and a narrow latent state, sixty-four numbers.
say: Each cell of a fifty kilometre grid carries a wide memory, five hundred and twelve numbers, and a narrow latent state, sixty-four numbers.
heard: Each cell of a 50-kilometer grid carries a wide memory, 512 numbers, and a narrow latent state, 64 numbers.

text: Each hour, the memory steps forward and guesses the latent state. That's the background.
say: Each hour, the memory steps forward and guesses the latent state. That's the background.
heard: Each hour, the memory steps forward and guesses the latent state. That's the background.

text: Then new observations arrive, and an attention step, reading them through the memory, corrects it. That's the analysis.
say: Then new observations arrive, and an attention step, reading them through the memory, corrects it. That's the analysis.
heard: Then new observations arrive, and an attention step, reading them through the memory, corrects it. That's the analysis.

text: Decoders translate the latent state into what any instrument would see, anywhere. Nobody writes down the gain.
say: Decoders translate the latent state into what any instrument would see, anywhere. Nobody writes down the gain.
heard: Decoders translate the latent state into what any instrument would see, anywhere. Nobody writes down the gain.

text: And there is no answer key. It trains on four years of raw observations from eighteen observing systems.
say: And there is no answer key. It trains on four years of raw observations from eighteen observing systems.
heard: And there is no answer key. It trains on four years of raw observations from 18 observing systems.

text: No reanalysis, the physics-built record that most AI weather models learn from, and whose biases they inherit.
say: No reanalysis, the physics-built record that most AI weather models learn from, and whose biases they inherit.
heard: No reanalysis, the physics-built record that most AI weather models learn from, and whose biases they inherit.

text: From one shared latent state, it can paint stations, balloons and satellite channels across the whole globe.
say: From one shared latent state, it can paint stations, balloons and satellite channels across the whole globe.
heard: From one shared latent state, it can paint stations, balloons, and satellite channels across the whole globe.

text: Earlier models also skipped reanalysis, but built each forecast in one pass, with no running memory. Keeping the loop is what's new.
say: Earlier models also skipped reanalysis, but built each forecast in one pass, with no running memory. Keeping the loop is what's new.
heard: Earlier models also skipped reanalysis, but built each forecast in one pass with no running memory. Keeping the loop is what's new.

text: Three lessons train it. One: rebuild what the instruments saw, including whole instruments hidden on purpose.
say: Three lessons train it. One: rebuild what the instruments saw, including whole instruments hidden on purpose.
heard: Three lessons train it. One, rebuild what the instruments saw, including whole instruments hidden on purpose.

text: Two: make the guess before each hour match the picture after it. The only way is to anticipate the observations.
say: Two: make the guess before each hour match the picture after it. The only way is to anticipate the observations.
heard: Two, make the guess before each hour match the picture after it. The only way is to anticipate the observations.

text: Three: run alone for hours, as an ensemble, scored on how well its spread of futures matches what happened.
say: Three: run alone for hours, as an ensemble, scored on how well its spread of futures matches what happened.
heard: Three, run alone for hours, as an ensemble, scored on how well its spread of futures matches what happened.

text: Does it work? At five hundred and thirty-four stations it never sees, forecasts run twelve hours ahead.
say: Does it work? At five hundred and thirty-four stations it never sees, forecasts run twelve hours ahead.
heard: Does it work? At 534 stations it never sees, forecasts run 12 hours ahead.

text: For wind, it beats both the American and the European ensembles at every hour.
say: For wind, it beats both the American and the European ensembles at every hour.
heard: For wind, it beats both the American and the European ensembles at every hour.

text: For temperature, it beats the American one throughout, and the European one for eight hours, before the European ensemble pulls ahead.
say: For temperature, it beats the American one throughout, and the European one for eight hours, before the European ensemble pulls ahead.
heard: For temperature, it beats the American one throughout, and the European one for eight hours, before the European ensemble pulls ahead.

text: And its spread of possible outcomes matches its real errors far better than either, though all three are still overconfident.

heard: And its spread of possible outcomes matches its real errors far better than either, though all three are still overconfident.

text: Rain, sunlight and cloud tops are never fed in. It reads them out of the latent state.
say: Rain, sunlight and cloud tops are never fed in. It reads them out of the latent state.
heard: Rain, sunlight, and cloud tops are never fed in. It reads them out of the latent state.

text: For rain, it's the best ensemble for six hours, though too dry and too smooth.
say: For rain, it's the best ensemble for six hours, though too dry and too smooth.
heard: For rain, it's the best ensemble for six hours, though too dry and too smooth.

text: Cloud tops, checked against a radar and laser satellite it never trained on, come out a little more accurate than the operational product. It raises half the false alarms, though it misses a little more real cloud.
say: Cloud tops, checked against a radar and laser satellite it never trained on, come out a little more accurate than the operational product. It raises half the false alarms, though it misses a little more real cloud.
heard: Cloud tops, checked against a radar and laser satellite it never trained on, come out a little more accurate than the operational product. It raises half the false alarms, though it misses a little more real cloud.

text: But here is the turn. Compare its forecasts a few hours ahead with NOAA's own assimilation, on the same observations.
say: But here is the turn. Compare its forecasts a few hours ahead with NOAA's own assimilation, on the same observations.
heard: But here is the turn. Compare its forecasts a few hours ahead with NOAA's own assimilation on the same observations.

text: At surface stations, the two are within about ten percent.

heard: At surface stations, the two are within about 10%.

text: Higher up, it falls behind. Balloon winds are two point six times worse on average, and satellite temperature channels up to about four and a half times.
